newsitem.title: UK: Britain says cases of mad cow disease declining.
newsitem.headline: Britain says cases of mad cow disease declining.

text.p: Cases of mad cow disease in Britain have declined by two-thirds in the last two years, the government said on Friday.
Junior agriculture minister Bernard Donoughue said the figures in a new report on bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) showed major improvements which were expected to continue.

"The number of clinically suspect cases of BSE reported in Great Britain has continued to fall and at June 30, 1997 was 56 percent less than at the same time in 1996 and 70 percent less than at the same time in 1995," he said in a House of Lords written reply.

The European Union banned British beef exports a year ago when scientists said a new form of Creutzfedlt-Jakob disease (CJD), a normally rare human equivalent of BSE, had been identified. They said eating infected beef products was the likely cause.
Scientists believe BSE was spread by the practice of feeding animal byproducts to cattle.
In the past decade the BSE epidemic had ravaged British cattle and more than 167,000 cases had been reported.
Donoughue said the government planned to introduce a computerised cattle tracing system as soon as possible to follow cases of the disease.
"Work is now underway, including discussions on detailed points of implementation with the livestock industry," he added.
